title: Maximum Vacation Days
statement:
You plan a trip of `k` weeks across `n` cities numbered `0` to `n - 1`, and you start in city `0`.

- `flights` is an `n x n` matrix: `flights[i][j] == 1` means a direct flight goes from city `i` to city `j`, and `0` means it does not. Flights are one-way, so the matrix need not be symmetric, and `flights[i][i]` is always `0`.
- `days` is an `n x k` matrix: `days[i][j]` is the most vacation days you can take if you spend week `j` in city `i`. Any other days of that week are work days.
- Travel happens only on the Monday morning that opens each week, the first week included. At that moment you either stay where you are or take exactly one direct flight out of your current city. Flight time is ignored, so the whole week (that Monday included) counts as spent in the city you end up in.

Return the largest total number of vacation days you can collect over the `k` weeks.
notes:
## Intuition

Brute force tries every itinerary, which is up to n choices per week, n^k plans in total. But the best you can do from some week onward depends only on **which city you are in** when that week starts, not on how you got there. That makes a table `dp[week][city]` that can be filled from the last week backwards.

## Approach

1. Make `dp` with `k + 1` rows of `n` zeros. Row `k` stands for "the trip is over", so it stays 0.
2. Go through the weeks from `k - 1` down to `0`.
3. For each starting `city`, try every `dest` you could spend the week in: `city` itself, or any city with `flights[city][dest] === 1`.
4. Spending week `week` in `dest` gives `days[dest][week]` now plus `dp[week + 1][dest]` for the rest of the trip. Keep the largest such `total` in `dp[week][city]`.
5. You start in city 0 before week 0, so return `dp[0][0]`.

## Example 1, step by step

Every pair of cities is linked, so each week you may pick any city.

- Week 2: the best single week is `max(1, 3, 3) = 3`, so `dp[2] = [3, 3, 3]`.
- Week 1: `days[dest][1]` is `3, 0, 3`; adding 3 gives at best 6, so `dp[1] = [6, 6, 6]`.
- Week 0: `days[dest][0]` is `1, 6, 3`; city 1 gives `6 + 6 = 12`, so `dp[0][0] = 12`.

One such plan: fly to city 1 (6 days), then to city 2 (3 days), then stay (3 days).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · k): each of the k weeks checks every (city, dest) pair once.
- Space: O(n · k) for the table; keeping only two rows would cut it to O(n).

## Pitfalls

- Staying put is always allowed even though `flights[city][city]` is 0; test `dest === city` separately.
- Flights are one-way: read `flights[city][dest]`, not `flights[dest][city]`.
- A forward DP must mark cities you cannot reach yet; the backward table avoids that because every city's future is well defined.
- The answer is `dp[0][0]`, not the largest value in row 0: the trip starts in city 0.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n`, `k` | number of cities and number of weeks |
| `dp[week][city]` | most vacation days from `week` to the end when that week starts in `city` |
| `week` | the week being decided, processed from last to first |
| `city` | where you are on that week's Monday morning |
| `dest` | where you spend that week (stay or one flight) |
| `total` | vacation days if the week is spent in `dest` |

narration.2: Count the cities from the size of flights.
narration.3: Count the weeks from the length of any days row.
narration.4: dp[week][city] will hold the best vacation total from week onward when starting it in city; row k means no weeks left.
narration.6: Fill the table from the last week back to the first, so later weeks are already known.
narration.7: Consider every city you might be in on this week's Monday.
narration.8: Consider every city you might spend the week in.
narration.9: You may stay where you are or take a direct flight out of city.
narration.10: Vacation days this week in dest plus the best possible from next week, starting in dest.
narration.11: Keep the best choice for this starting city.
narration.16: The trip starts in city 0 before week 0, so this cell is the answer.
